This is a draft research paper for a prototype built for an IEEE student competition. The system was evaluated in a controlled setup and with simulated signals. It was not validated with wild elephants or deer on a live road. All statements about road safety impact must be sourced from verified data before submission. Results marked [TO FILL] must be taken from the test records.
Abstract

Wild animals crossing highways are a recurring hazard in Sri Lanka, and collisions with elephants and deer endanger drivers, passengers and the animals themselves. Conventional mitigation, such as fencing and signage, is costly to maintain across long road lengths and does not warn drivers in real time. This paper describes a low-cost early-warning prototype that combines two sensing modalities: an infrared beam-break sensor array to detect crossing events, and a geophone to detect the ground vibration produced by large animals moving nearby. An Arduino handles sensor sampling and thresholding, and a Raspberry Pi performs event fusion and alert generation. The paper presents the design, the detection logic that combines the two modalities, and a controlled evaluation using staged crossings and recorded vibration signatures. The evaluation measures detection rate, false-alarm rate and alert latency. The results are preliminary and establish feasibility under controlled conditions. They do not establish performance on a live road, which requires field trials.
1. Introduction

Large wild animals move across Sri Lankan roads, and when they do, the consequences can be fatal. The problem is a combination of predictable crossing corridors, limited warning for drivers, and long road sections that are difficult to monitor. Fixed signage informs drivers in general, but does not indicate that an animal is present at a given moment.

An early-warning system addresses the timing gap. If the presence of an animal near the road can be detected a short distance ahead of the crossing, a warning can be displayed to approaching drivers, and the warning can be targeted to the section of road where the risk is current. The design goal is a system that is cheap to build, simple to maintain, and able to run unattended.

This paper makes three contributions. It describes a two-modality prototype using low-cost components. It defines a fusion rule that uses the beam-break and vibration signals together, so that either signal alone cannot trigger an alert. And it reports a controlled evaluation of detection and false-alarm behaviour, with clear limits on what that evaluation shows.
2. Related Work

Wildlife-vehicle collision mitigation includes fencing, underpasses, animal detection systems, and driver warning signs. Camera-based animal detection has been widely studied, but it depends on lighting, needs significant processing, and can be affected by weather and vegetation. Radar and thermal sensing offer better performance in some conditions, but at higher cost.

Seismic and vibration sensing has been used to detect human and vehicle footsteps and to monitor large animal movement, because large mammals transmit energy into the ground. Vibration sensing is independent of lighting, but it is sensitive to other sources, including traffic, wind and machinery. Combining vibration with a second, independent modality reduces false alarms from any single source. 3. System Design
3.1 Architecture

The system has two sensing nodes and a processing unit. Each node includes an Arduino board that samples its sensors. The processing unit is a Raspberry Pi that receives events from both nodes, applies the fusion rule, and generates alerts. Communication between the Arduino nodes and the Raspberry Pi is [TO FILL: serial, wired or wireless protocol].
3.2 Infrared Beam-Break Module

An infrared emitter and receiver pair forms a beam across the expected crossing path. An interruption of the beam, lasting longer than a minimum duration, is recorded as a crossing candidate. The minimum duration filters out small objects and brief disturbances. [TO FILL: beam length, mounting height, emitter and receiver models, and the minimum duration used.]
3.3 Seismic Vibration Module

A geophone, coupled to the ground, records vibration. The Arduino samples the signal, computes a short-window amplitude measure, and flags a vibration event when the measure exceeds a threshold that was set from background recordings. [TO FILL: geophone model, sampling rate, window length, and how the threshold was set.]

Geophones measure ground velocity and are sensitive to nearby traffic, so the threshold and frequency band are important design choices. [TO FILL: state the frequency band used and any filtering applied.]
3.4 Fusion Rule

An alert is generated only when a beam-break event and a vibration event occur within a defined time window. A beam break without vibration may be a small object or a fault, and vibration without a beam break may be traffic or wind. Requiring both reduces false alarms, at the cost of possibly missing an animal that crosses without a strong vibration signal. This trade-off is discussed in Section 6.

Tests were run under [TO FILL: lighting conditions, background noise, and whether traffic was simulated]. Each condition was repeated [TO FILL: number of trials per condition].
4.3 Measures

The evaluation records four measures. Detection rate is the proportion of staged crossings that produced an alert. False-alarm rate is the number of alerts produced when no crossing was staged, per hour of background operation. Alert latency is the time from the start of the crossing to the alert. And for each modality on its own, the detection rate is recorded to show the contribution of the fusion rule.
4.4 Simulation Limitations

Staged and simulated crossings differ from real animal movement in speed, weight, path, and the ground vibration produced. The results can therefore indicate whether the logic works, but cannot predict real detection performance. This is the main limitation of the evaluation.

6. Discussion

The results support the feasibility of the two-modality design under controlled conditions. The fusion rule reduces false alarms relative to each modality alone, if [TO FILL: confirm from results]. The main trade-off is that requiring both modalities may miss an animal that crosses quietly or on a soft surface. Whether that trade-off is acceptable depends on the road, the animal, and the cost of a missed alert compared with a false one, which requires a field study to judge.

The practical deployment questions are separate from the feasibility question. Power supply for remote sections, weatherproofing, maintenance, theft and vandalism, and the design of the warning output for drivers all need work. Early-warning systems also depend on the response of drivers and of the authorities who maintain the road, and this paper does not evaluate that response.
7. Limitations

The evaluation used staged crossings and controlled conditions, and no live road or wild animal was included. The sample size was [TO FILL: n]. The vibration signature of a real elephant or deer was not measured. The system was designed and evaluated by a single author, with the testing approved informally, not by a formal ethics or road-authority process. Long-term reliability, environmental durability and field maintenance were not assessed.
8. Conclusion

The paper describes a low-cost early-warning prototype that combines infrared beam-break and geophone vibration sensing, with a fusion rule designed to reduce false alarms. The controlled evaluation shows that the logic works under simulated conditions. The next step is a field study on a real road section, with the appropriate permissions from the road and wildlife authorities, measuring performance against real animal crossings.
